questions.q: A block rests on a rough wedge of angle $30^{\circ}$. The wedge is given a horizontal acceleration of $g\sqrt{3}$ to the right, and the block is found to be on the verge of sliding up the incline. The minimum coefficient of static friction required to prevent the block from sliding up the wedge is
questions.question: A block rests on a rough wedge of angle $30^{\circ}$. The wedge is given a horizontal acceleration of $g\sqrt{3}$ to the right, and the block is found to be on the verge of sliding up the incline. The minimum coefficient of static friction required to prevent the block from sliding up the wedge is
questions.solution:
In the reference frame of the wedge, a pseudo force $ma$ acts on the block horizontally to the left.

Resolving the forces perpendicular to the inclined plane, the normal reaction is:
$N = mg \cos 30^{\circ} + ma \sin 30^{\circ}$

Substituting $a = g\sqrt{3}$:
$N = mg \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) + m(g\sqrt{3}) \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{3}mg$

The net driving force pushing the block up the incline is:
$F_{\text{up}} = ma \cos 30^{\circ} - mg \sin 30^{\circ}$

$F_{\text{up}} = m(g\sqrt{3}) \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) - mg \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \dfrac{3mg}{2} - \dfrac{mg}{2} = mg$

For the block to be on the verge of sliding up, the limiting friction must balance this upward force:
$F_{\text{up}} = \mu_s N$

$mg = \mu_s (\sqrt{3}mg)$

$\mu_s = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

A machine of mass $20\text{ kg}$ is pushed across a horizontal floor by a force $F$ directed at an angle of $37^{\circ}$ below the horizontal. The machine moves with a constant velocity. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the machine and the floor is $0.5$, the magnitude of the pushing force $F$ is
(Given $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = 0.6$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = 0.8$)
questions.question:
A machine of mass $20\text{ kg}$ is pushed across a horizontal floor by a force $F$ directed at an angle of $37^{\circ}$ below the horizontal. The machine moves with a constant velocity. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the machine and the floor is $0.5$, the magnitude of the pushing force $F$ is
(Given $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = 0.6$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = 0.8$)
questions.solution:
Let $N$ be the normal reaction from the floor.
Resolving the pushing force $F$ into horizontal and vertical components, we get $F \cos 37^{\circ}$ horizontally and $F \sin 37^{\circ}$ vertically downwards.

For vertical equilibrium:
$N = Mg + F \sin 37^{\circ}$
$N = 20 \times 10 + F(0.6) = 200 + 0.6F$

Since the machine moves with constant velocity, the net horizontal force is zero. Thus, the horizontal component of the pushing force equals the kinetic friction:
$F \cos 37^{\circ} = \mu_k N$
$F(0.8) = 0.5(200 + 0.6F)$
$0.8F = 100 + 0.3F$
$0.5F = 100$
$F = 200\text{ N}$

Answer: $200\text{ N}$

questions.q: A particle of mass $3\text{ kg}$ moves along the positive $x$-axis under the influence of a constant force. The variation of the square of its velocity ($v^2$) with position ($x$) is represented by a straight line passing through the origin and the point $(4\text{ m}, 16\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2)$. The magnitude of the force acting on the particle is :
questions.question: A particle of mass $3\text{ kg}$ moves along the positive $x$-axis under the influence of a constant force. The variation of the square of its velocity ($v^2$) with position ($x$) is represented by a straight line passing through the origin and the point $(4\text{ m}, 16\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2)$. The magnitude of the force acting on the particle is :
questions.solution:
The graph of $v^2$ versus $x$ is a straight line passing through $(0,0)$ and $(4, 16)$.

The slope of this line is $k = \dfrac{16 - 0}{4 - 0} = 4\text{ m/s}^2$.

The equation of the line is $v^2 = 4x$.

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ gives:
$2v \dfrac{dv}{dx} = 4$

Since acceleration $a = v \dfrac{dv}{dx}$, we have:
$2a = 4 \Rightarrow a = 2\text{ m/s}^2$

The magnitude of the constant force is:
$F = ma = 3 \times 2 = 6\text{ N}$

Answer: $6\text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is projected upwards along a rough inclined plane of angle $60^{\circ}$. It momentarily comes to rest and then slides back down to its starting point. If the time taken by the block to slide down is twice the time taken to slide up, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is :
questions.question: A block is projected upwards along a rough inclined plane of angle $60^{\circ}$. It momentarily comes to rest and then slides back down to its starting point. If the time taken by the block to slide down is twice the time taken to slide up, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is :
questions.solution:
Let the distance moved along the incline be $d$.

During the upward motion, friction acts downwards. The retardation is:
$a_{\text{up}} = g(\sin 60^{\circ} + \mu_k \cos 60^{\circ})$

Using $d = \dfrac{1}{2} a_{\text{up}} t_{\text{up}}^2$ (analyzing the ascent in reverse from the highest point where velocity is zero).

During the downward motion, friction acts upwards. The acceleration is:
$a_{\text{down}} = g(\sin 60^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 60^{\circ})$

Using $d = \dfrac{1}{2} a_{\text{down}} t_{\text{down}}^2$.

Equating the two expressions for $d$:
$\dfrac{1}{2} a_{\text{up}} t_{\text{up}}^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} a_{\text{down}} t_{\text{down}}^2$

$\dfrac{a_{\text{up}}}{a_{\text{down}}} = \left(\dfrac{t_{\text{down}}}{t_{\text{up}}}\right)^2$

Given $t_{\text{down}} = 2 t_{\text{up}}$, we get:
$\dfrac{a_{\text{up}}}{a_{\text{down}}} = 4$

Substituting the expressions for acceleration:
$\dfrac{g(\sin 60^{\circ} + \mu_k \cos 60^{\circ})}{g(\sin 60^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 60^{\circ})} = 4$

$\dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \mu_k \dfrac{1}{2}}{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \mu_k \dfrac{1}{2}} = 4$

$\sqrt{3} + \mu_k = 4(\sqrt{3} - \mu_k)$

$\sqrt{3} + \mu_k = 4\sqrt{3} - 4\mu_k$

$5\mu_k = 3\sqrt{3}$

$\mu_k = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{5}$

questions.q: In a 'Rotor' amusement park ride, riders stand against the inner wall of a rotating vertical cylinder. Once the cylinder reaches a certain speed, the floor drops away. If the cylinder rotates at a constant angular speed of $2$ rad/s and the coefficient of static friction between a rider's clothing and the wall is $0.5$, what is the minimum radius of the cylinder required to prevent the riders from sliding down? (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.question: In a 'Rotor' amusement park ride, riders stand against the inner wall of a rotating vertical cylinder. Once the cylinder reaches a certain speed, the floor drops away. If the cylinder rotates at a constant angular speed of $2$ rad/s and the coefficient of static friction between a rider's clothing and the wall is $0.5$, what is the minimum radius of the cylinder required to prevent the riders from sliding down? (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
The normal force $N$ exerted by the wall on the rider provides the necessary centripetal force:

$N = m \omega^2 R$

For the rider not to slide down, the upward static friction $f$ must balance the downward gravitational force $mg$. The maximum available static friction is $\mu N$. Therefore, the condition to prevent sliding is:

$mg \le \mu N$

$mg \le \mu (m \omega^2 R)$

The mass $m$ cancels out from both sides:

$g \le \mu \omega^2 R$

Rearranging for the radius $R$:

$R \ge \dfrac{g}{\mu \omega^2}$

Substitute the given values $g = 10$ m/s$^2$, $\mu = 0.5$, and $\omega = 2$ rad/s:

$R \ge \dfrac{10}{0.5 \times (2)^2}$

$R \ge \dfrac{10}{0.5 \times 4}$

$R \ge \dfrac{10}{2}$

$R \ge 5$ m

The minimum radius of the cylinder is $5$ m.

Answer: $5$ m

questions.q: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ starts from the origin at $t=0$. Its velocity vector as a function of time is given by $\vec{v}(t) = (3t^2 \hat{i} + 4t \hat{j})\text{ m/s}$. The net force vector acting on the particle at the exact instant its $x$-coordinate reaches $8\text{ m}$ is:
questions.question: A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ starts from the origin at $t=0$. Its velocity vector as a function of time is given by $\vec{v}(t) = (3t^2 \hat{i} + 4t \hat{j})\text{ m/s}$. The net force vector acting on the particle at the exact instant its $x$-coordinate reaches $8\text{ m}$ is:
questions.solution:
Given the velocity vector $\vec{v}(t) = 3t^2 \hat{i} + 4t \hat{j}$, the $x$-component of velocity is $v_x = 3t^2$.

The $x$-coordinate as a function of time is found by integrating $v_x$ with respect to time:
$x(t) = \int 3t^2 dt = t^3$
(since it starts from the origin, the constant of integration is zero).

We are given that the target $x$-coordinate is $8\text{ m}$. Setting $x(t) = 8$ gives:
$t^3 = 8 \implies t = 2\text{ s}$.

Next, we find the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector with respect to time:
$\vec{a}(t) = \dfrac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = 6t \hat{i} + 4 \hat{j}$

At $t = 2\text{ s}$, the acceleration is:
$\vec{a} = 6(2) \hat{i} + 4 \hat{j} = 12 \hat{i} + 4 \hat{j}\text{ m/s}^2$

According to Newton's Second Law, the net force is $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$. With $m = 2\text{ kg}$:
$\vec{F} = 2(12 \hat{i} + 4 \hat{j}) = (24 \hat{i} + 8 \hat{j})\text{ N}$.

Answer: $(24 \hat{i} + 8 \hat{j})\text{ N}$

questions.q: A block of mass $m_1$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a hanging block of mass $m_2$. When the system is released from rest, the tension in the string is found to be one-fourth of the weight of the block of mass $m_1$. The ratio of the masses $\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}$ is
questions.question: A block of mass $m_1$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a hanging block of mass $m_2$. When the system is released from rest, the tension in the string is found to be one-fourth of the weight of the block of mass $m_1$. The ratio of the masses $\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}$ is
questions.solution:
Let the acceleration of the system be $a$.

The equations of motion for the blocks are:
For mass $m_1$ on the table: $T = m_1 a$
For hanging mass $m_2$: $m_2 g - T = m_2 a$

Adding these equations gives the acceleration:
$a = \dfrac{m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$

Substituting $a$ back into the first equation, the tension is:
$T = \dfrac{m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$

We are given that the tension is one-fourth of the weight of $m_1$:
$T = \dfrac{m_1 g}{4}$

Equating the two expressions for tension:
$\dfrac{m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{m_1 g}{4}$

Cancelling $m_1 g$ from both sides:
$\dfrac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Cross-multiplying yields:
$4 m_2 = m_1 + m_2$
$3 m_2 = m_1$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.q: An Atwood machine consists of two blocks of masses $M_1$ and $M_2$ ($M_1 > M_2$) connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley. The system is released from rest and the heavier mass $M_1$ moves downwards with an acceleration $a$. If a small mass $m$ is removed from $M_1$ and attached to $M_2$, the system moves with a constant velocity. If instead, the same mass $m$ is removed from $M_2$ and attached to $M_1$, the downward acceleration of the heavier side becomes $a'$. The ratio $\dfrac{a'}{a}$ is
questions.question: An Atwood machine consists of two blocks of masses $M_1$ and $M_2$ ($M_1 > M_2$) connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley. The system is released from rest and the heavier mass $M_1$ moves downwards with an acceleration $a$. If a small mass $m$ is removed from $M_1$ and attached to $M_2$, the system moves with a constant velocity. If instead, the same mass $m$ is removed from $M_2$ and attached to $M_1$, the downward acceleration of the heavier side becomes $a'$. The ratio $\dfrac{a'}{a}$ is
questions.solution:
Let the total mass of the system be $M = M_1 + M_2$.
The initial acceleration of the system is given by:
$a = \dfrac{M_1 - M_2}{M_1 + M_2}g$

When mass $m$ is transferred from $M_1$ to $M_2$, the new masses are $(M_1 - m)$ and $(M_2 + m)$. The system moves with constant velocity, which means the net force is zero (acceleration is zero).
$\Rightarrow (M_1 - m)g = (M_2 + m)g$
$\Rightarrow M_1 - M_2 = 2m$
Substituting this into the initial acceleration equation:
$a = \dfrac{2m}{M}g$

When mass $m$ is instead transferred from $M_2$ to $M_1$, the new masses become $(M_1 + m)$ and $(M_2 - m)$. The new acceleration $a'$ is:
$a' = \dfrac{(M_1 + m) - (M_2 - m)}{M_1 + M_2}g$
$a' = \dfrac{M_1 - M_2 + 2m}{M}g$

Since $M_1 - M_2 = 2m$, we can substitute this into the expression for $a'$:
$a' = \dfrac{2m + 2m}{M}g = \dfrac{4m}{M}g$

Taking the ratio of the two accelerations:
$\dfrac{a'}{a} = \dfrac{\dfrac{4m}{M}g}{\dfrac{2m}{M}g} = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is pressed against a rough vertical wall by applying a constant horizontal force $F$. If the block slides downwards along the wall with a constant velocity, the magnitude of the total contact force exerted by the wall on the block is :
questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is pressed against a rough vertical wall by applying a constant horizontal force $F$. If the block slides downwards along the wall with a constant velocity, the magnitude of the total contact force exerted by the wall on the block is :
questions.solution:
Since the block moves with a constant velocity, its acceleration is zero, and the net force acting on it must be zero.

In the horizontal direction, the normal force $N$ exerted by the wall balances the applied force $F$. Thus, $N = F$.

In the vertical direction, the upward kinetic friction $f$ balances the downward weight of the block. Thus, $f = mg$.

The total contact force exerted by the wall is the vector sum of the normal force and the frictional force. Since they are perpendicular to each other, its magnitude is:
$F_{\text{contact}} = \sqrt{N^2 + f^2} = \sqrt{F^2 + m^2g^2}$

Answer: $\sqrt{F^2 + m^2g^2}$

questions.q: Two blocks of masses $2\text{ kg}$ and $3\text{ kg}$ are placed on a smooth horizontal surface and connected by a light elastic string. When a constant horizontal force of $15\text{ N}$ is applied to the $3\text{ kg}$ block, the steady-state length of the string is $44\text{ cm}$. When the same horizontal force is instead applied to the $2\text{ kg}$ block, the steady-state length of the string becomes $47\text{ cm}$. The natural length of the string is _____ cm.
questions.question: Two blocks of masses $2\text{ kg}$ and $3\text{ kg}$ are placed on a smooth horizontal surface and connected by a light elastic string. When a constant horizontal force of $15\text{ N}$ is applied to the $3\text{ kg}$ block, the steady-state length of the string is $44\text{ cm}$. When the same horizontal force is instead applied to the $2\text{ kg}$ block, the steady-state length of the string becomes $47\text{ cm}$. The natural length of the string is _____ cm.
questions.solution:
Let the natural length of the string be $L_0$ and its stiffness constant be $k$.

The acceleration of the system in both cases is:
$a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{15}{2 + 3} = 3\text{ m/s}^2$

Case 1: The force is applied to the $3\text{ kg}$ block.
The tension $T_1$ in the string is responsible for accelerating the trailing $2\text{ kg}$ block.
$T_1 = m_1 a = 2 \times 3 = 6\text{ N}$
Using Hooke's law:
$6 = k(44 - L_0)$

Case 2: The force is applied to the $2\text{ kg}$ block.
The tension $T_2$ in the string is responsible for accelerating the trailing $3\text{ kg}$ block.
$T_2 = m_2 a = 3 \times 3 = 9\text{ N}$
Using Hooke's law:
$9 = k(47 - L_0)$

Dividing the first equation by the second:
$\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{44 - L_0}{47 - L_0}$

$\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{44 - L_0}{47 - L_0}$

$2(47 - L_0) = 3(44 - L_0)$
$94 - 2L_0 = 132 - 3L_0$
$L_0 = 132 - 94 = 38\text{ cm}$

Answer: $38$

questions.q: A body of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is attached to the lower end of a spring of natural length $0.6\text{ m}$ and spring constant $100\text{ N m}^{-1}$. The upper end of the spring is fixed to a rigid ceiling. The body is made to move in a horizontal circle such that the spring acts as a conical pendulum, maintaining a constant angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the vertical. Taking $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, the constant angular speed of the body is:
questions.question: A body of mass $1\text{ kg}$ is attached to the lower end of a spring of natural length $0.6\text{ m}$ and spring constant $100\text{ N m}^{-1}$. The upper end of the spring is fixed to a rigid ceiling. The body is made to move in a horizontal circle such that the spring acts as a conical pendulum, maintaining a constant angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the vertical. Taking $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, the constant angular speed of the body is:
questions.solution:
Let the extension in the spring be $x$. The spring force is $F_s = kx$.

In the vertical direction, the component of the spring force balances the weight of the body:
$kx \cos\theta = mg$
$100 \times x \times \cos(60^{\circ}) = 1 \times 10$
$100 \times x \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 10 \Rightarrow 50x = 10 \Rightarrow x = 0.2\text{ m}$

The radius $R$ of the horizontal circular path is the horizontal component of the stretched spring's length:
$R = (l + x) \sin\theta$
$R = (0.6 + 0.2) \sin(60^{\circ}) = 0.8 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0.4\sqrt{3}\text{ m}$

In the horizontal direction, the component of the spring force provides the necessary centripetal force:
$kx \sin\theta = mR\omega^2$
$100 \times 0.2 \times \sin(60^{\circ}) = 1 \times (0.4\sqrt{3}) \times \omega^2$
$20 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0.4\sqrt{3} \times \omega^2$
$10\sqrt{3} = 0.4\sqrt{3} \times \omega^2$
$\omega^2 = \dfrac{10}{0.4} = 25$
$\omega = 5\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Answer: $5\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

questions.q: Three blocks A, B, and C are connected in series by massless strings and placed on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal pulling force is applied to block C, causing the entire system to accelerate. The mass of the trailing block A is $2\text{ kg}$. If the tension in the string connecting blocks B and C is exactly three times the tension in the string connecting blocks A and B, what is the mass of block B?
questions.question: Three blocks A, B, and C are connected in series by massless strings and placed on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal pulling force is applied to block C, causing the entire system to accelerate. The mass of the trailing block A is $2\text{ kg}$. If the tension in the string connecting blocks B and C is exactly three times the tension in the string connecting blocks A and B, what is the mass of block B?
questions.solution:
Let the common acceleration of the system be $a$.

The tension $T_1$ in the string between blocks A and B is responsible for accelerating only block A.
$T_1 = m_A a$

The tension $T_2$ in the string between blocks B and C is responsible for accelerating both blocks A and B.
$T_2 = (m_A + m_B) a$

Given that $T_2 = 3T_1$, we have:
$(m_A + m_B) a = 3(m_A a)$

Since $a \neq 0$, we can divide by $a$:
$m_A + m_B = 3m_A$
$m_B = 2m_A$

Given $m_A = 2\text{ kg}$, we find:
$m_B = 2 \times 2\text{ kg} = 4\text{ kg}$

Answer: $4\text{ kg}$

questions.q: A block of mass $M$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth, massless pulley at the edge of the table to a hanging block of mass $m$. When $m = \dfrac{M}{3}$, the acceleration of the system is $a_1$. When $m = \dfrac{M}{2}$, the acceleration of the system is $a_2$. The ratio $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}$ is
questions.question: A block of mass $M$ rests on a smooth horizontal table. It is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth, massless pulley at the edge of the table to a hanging block of mass $m$. When $m = \dfrac{M}{3}$, the acceleration of the system is $a_1$. When $m = \dfrac{M}{2}$, the acceleration of the system is $a_2$. The ratio $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}$ is
questions.solution:
For a system where a block of mass $M$ is on a smooth horizontal table and is pulled by a hanging mass $m$, the driving force is the weight of the hanging mass, $mg$.
The total mass being accelerated is $(M + m)$.
Therefore, the acceleration of the system is:
$a = \dfrac{mg}{M + m}$

Case 1: When $m = \dfrac{M}{3}$
$a_1 = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{M}{3}\right)g}{M + \dfrac{M}{3}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{M}{3}}{\dfrac{4M}{3}}g = \dfrac{g}{4}$

Case 2: When $m = \dfrac{M}{2}$
$a_2 = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{M}{2}\right)g}{M + \dfrac{M}{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{M}{2}}{\dfrac{3M}{2}}g = \dfrac{g}{3}$

Taking the ratio of the two accelerations:
$\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{g}{4}}{\dfrac{g}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is sliding on a rough horizontal surface. The velocity-time graph of the block's motion is a straight line. The graph intersects the velocity axis at $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the time axis at $4\text{ s}$. The value of the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question:
A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is sliding on a rough horizontal surface. The velocity-time graph of the block's motion is a straight line. The graph intersects the velocity axis at $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the time axis at $4\text{ s}$. The value of the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
From the velocity-time graph, the initial velocity is $u = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the final velocity is $v = 0$ at $t = 4\text{ s}$.

The magnitude of deceleration is given by the slope of the velocity-time graph:
$a = \dfrac{12 - 0}{4} = 3\text{ m s}^{-2}$

The only horizontal force acting on the block is the kinetic friction, which provides the deceleration.
$f_k = m a$
$\mu_k m g = m a$
$\mu_k = \dfrac{a}{g}$

Substituting the values:
$\mu_k = \dfrac{3}{10} = 0.3$

Answer: $0.3$

questions.q: A block of mass $5$ kg is sliding at a speed of $5$ m/s on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is $0.2$. A constant horizontal force is applied on the block in the direction of its motion. If the block covers a distance of $44$ m in the next $4$ s, the magnitude of the applied force is (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$):
questions.question: A block of mass $5$ kg is sliding at a speed of $5$ m/s on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is $0.2$. A constant horizontal force is applied on the block in the direction of its motion. If the block covers a distance of $44$ m in the next $4$ s, the magnitude of the applied force is (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$):
questions.solution:
From the second equation of motion,

$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

$\Rightarrow 44 = 5(4) + \dfrac{1}{2}a(4)^2$

$\Rightarrow 44 = 20 + 8a$

$\Rightarrow a = 3$ m/s$^2$

The kinetic friction acting on the block is,

$f_k = \mu_k mg = 0.2 \times 5 \times 10 = 10$ N

Applying Newton's second law in the horizontal direction,

$F - f_k = ma$

$\Rightarrow F - 10 = 5 \times 3$

$\Rightarrow F = 25$ N

Answer: $25$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block is projected upwards along a rough inclined plane with an initial speed of $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The angle of inclination of the plane is $37^{\circ}$. If the block travels a distance of $5\text{ m}$ up the incline before momentarily coming to rest, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$)
questions.question:
A block is projected upwards along a rough inclined plane with an initial speed of $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The angle of inclination of the plane is $37^{\circ}$. If the block travels a distance of $5\text{ m}$ up the incline before momentarily coming to rest, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$)
questions.solution:
Using the kinematic equation for uniform acceleration:
$v^2 = u^2 - 2as$

Given $u = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, and $s = 5\text{ m}$:
$0 = (10)^2 - 2 \times a \times 5$
$10a = 100 \Rightarrow a = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$

For a block sliding up a rough inclined plane, the net deceleration is provided by the component of gravity and the kinetic friction acting downwards along the incline:
$m a = m g \sin \theta + \mu_k m g \cos \theta$
$a = g (\sin \theta + \mu_k \cos \theta)$

Substituting the given values:
$10 = 10 \left(\dfrac{3}{5} + \mu_k \times \dfrac{4}{5}\right)$
$1 = 0.6 + 0.8 \mu_k$
$0.8 \mu_k = 0.4$
$\mu_k = \dfrac{0.4}{0.8} = 0.5$

Answer: $0.5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A horizontal water jet strikes a block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal surface. The water falls vertically downwards immediately after striking the block. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the surface is $0.4$. If the velocity of the water jet is $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, the minimum rate of mass flow of water required to just start the motion of the block is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question:
A horizontal water jet strikes a block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal surface. The water falls vertically downwards immediately after striking the block. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the surface is $0.4$. If the velocity of the water jet is $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, the minimum rate of mass flow of water required to just start the motion of the block is:
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
For the block to just start moving, the force exerted by the water jet must be equal to the limiting static friction between the block and the surface.

The limiting static friction $f_{L}$ is:

$f_{L} = \mu M g$

Given $\mu = 0.4$, $M = 5\text{ kg}$, and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$:

$f_{L} = 0.4 \times 5 \times 10 = 20\text{ N}$

The force $F$ exerted by the horizontal water jet on the block is:

$F = v \dfrac{dm}{dt}$

where $v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is the velocity of the jet and $\dfrac{dm}{dt}$ is the rate of mass flow of water.

Equating the thrust force to the limiting friction:

$v \dfrac{dm}{dt} = f_{L}$

$10 \times \dfrac{dm}{dt} = 20$

$\dfrac{dm}{dt} = 2\text{ kg s}^{-1}$

Answer: $2\text{ kg s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block rests on the horizontal floor of an elevator that is accelerating upwards at $2 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. The block is suddenly given a horizontal velocity of $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ relative to the elevator floor. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is $0.5$, the distance the block slides relative to the floor before coming to rest is :
[Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.question:
A block rests on the horizontal floor of an elevator that is accelerating upwards at $2 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. The block is suddenly given a horizontal velocity of $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ relative to the elevator floor. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is $0.5$, the distance the block slides relative to the floor before coming to rest is :
[Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
In the non-inertial frame of the accelerating elevator, a pseudo force acts downwards on the block.
The effective acceleration due to gravity is $g' = g + a_e = 10 + 2 = 12 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

The normal force exerted by the floor on the block is $N = m g' = 12m$.
The kinetic friction acting on the block is $f_k = \mu N = 0.5 \times 12m = 6m$.

The horizontal deceleration of the block relative to the elevator is:
$a = \dfrac{f_k}{m} = 6 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Using the kinematic equation $v^2 = u^2 - 2as$ with final velocity $v = 0$ relative to the elevator:
$0 = (6)^2 - 2(6)s$
$12s = 36 \Rightarrow s = 3 \text{ m}$.

Answer: $3 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person of mass $80\text{ kg}$ needs to slide down a vertical rope. The rope can withstand a maximum tension of $600\text{ N}$ before breaking. What is the minimum downward acceleration with which the person must slide to ensure the rope does not break? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question: A person of mass $80\text{ kg}$ needs to slide down a vertical rope. The rope can withstand a maximum tension of $600\text{ N}$ before breaking. What is the minimum downward acceleration with which the person must slide to ensure the rope does not break? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the downward acceleration of the person.

The forces acting on the person are the gravitational force $mg$ downwards and the tension $T$ upwards.

Using Newton's second law for downward motion:
$mg - T = ma$

To prevent the rope from breaking, the tension $T$ must be less than or equal to the maximum breaking strength $T_{\text{max}}$.
$T \le 600\text{ N}$

From the equation of motion, $T = mg - ma$.
Therefore, $mg - ma \le 600$

Substitute the given values ($m = 80\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$):
$80(10) - 80a \le 600$
$800 - 80a \le 600$
$200 \le 80a$
$a \ge \dfrac{200}{80}$
$a \ge 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$

The minimum downward acceleration required is $2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Answer: $2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is projected up a rough inclined plane of angle $45^\circ$ with an initial speed $u$. It travels a distance $S_1$ before coming to rest. If the same block is projected with the same initial speed up a perfectly smooth inclined plane of the same angle, it travels a distance $S_2$ before coming to rest. If $S_1 : S_2 = 2 : 3$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the rough inclined plane is:
questions.question: A block is projected up a rough inclined plane of angle $45^\circ$ with an initial speed $u$. It travels a distance $S_1$ before coming to rest. If the same block is projected with the same initial speed up a perfectly smooth inclined plane of the same angle, it travels a distance $S_2$ before coming to rest. If $S_1 : S_2 = 2 : 3$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the rough inclined plane is:
questions.solution:
Let the angle of inclination be $\theta = 45^\circ$.

On the smooth inclined plane, the deceleration is $a_2 = g \sin\theta$.
Using the third equation of motion ($v^2 = u^2 - 2as$), the stopping distance is:
$S_2 = \dfrac{u^2}{2g \sin\theta}$

On the rough inclined plane, the deceleration is due to both gravity and kinetic friction:
$a_1 = g(\sin\theta + \mu_k \cos\theta)$
The stopping distance is:
$S_1 = \dfrac{u^2}{2g(\sin\theta + \mu_k \cos\theta)}$

Given the ratio $S_1 : S_2 = 2 : 3$, we have:
$\dfrac{S_1}{S_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{u^2}{2g(\sin\theta + \mu_k \cos\theta)}}{\dfrac{u^2}{2g \sin\theta}} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin\theta + \mu_k \cos\theta} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Substitute $\theta = 45^\circ$, noting that $\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$:
$\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \mu_k \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Dividing numerator and denominator by $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$:
$\dfrac{1}{1 + \mu_k} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Cross-multiplying yields:
$3 = 2(1 + \mu_k)$
$3 = 2 + 2\mu_k$
$2\mu_k = 1$
$\mu_k = 0.5$

Answer: $0.5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block $M$ of mass $40 \mathrm{~kg}$ rests on a smooth horizontal surface. A block $m_1$ of mass $10 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed on top of $M$ and is connected by a weightless, inextensible string passing over a smooth, light pulley fixed at the right edge of $M$, to a hanging block $m_2$ of mass $10 \mathrm{~kg}$. The block $m_2$ is in contact with the vertical right face of $M$. All surfaces are frictionless. A horizontal force $F = 380 \mathrm{~N}$ is applied to $M$ towards the right, causing $m_2$ to accelerate downwards relative to $M$. The downward acceleration of $m_2$ relative to $M$ is
(Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$)
questions.question:
A block $M$ of mass $40 \mathrm{~kg}$ rests on a smooth horizontal surface. A block $m_1$ of mass $10 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed on top of $M$ and is connected by a weightless, inextensible string passing over a smooth, light pulley fixed at the right edge of $M$, to a hanging block $m_2$ of mass $10 \mathrm{~kg}$. The block $m_2$ is in contact with the vertical right face of $M$. All surfaces are frictionless. A horizontal force $F = 380 \mathrm{~N}$ is applied to $M$ towards the right, causing $m_2$ to accelerate downwards relative to $M$. The downward acceleration of $m_2$ relative to $M$ is
(Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$)
questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the acceleration of block $M$ to the right, and $a_r$ be the downward acceleration of $m_2$ relative to $M$.

For block $m_2$ in the vertical direction:
$m_2 g - T = m_2 a_r$
$100 - T = 10 a_r$ ... (i)

For block $m_1$ in the horizontal direction (in the frame of $M$):
The pseudo force is $m_1 a$ to the left.
$T - m_1 a = m_1 a_r$
$T - 10 a = 10 a_r$ ... (ii)

Adding (i) and (ii):
$100 - 10 a = 20 a_r$
$\Rightarrow a = 10 - 2 a_r$ ... (iii)

Considering the horizontal motion of the entire system, the external force $F$ accelerates $M$ and $m_2$ at $a$, and $m_1$ at $(a + a_r)$ relative to the ground.
$F = M a + m_2 a + m_1 (a + a_r)$
$380 = 40 a + 10 a + 10 (a + a_r)$
$380 = 60 a + 10 a_r$
$38 = 6 a + a_r$ ... (iv)

Substituting (iii) into (iv):
$38 = 6 (10 - 2 a_r) + a_r$
$38 = 60 - 12 a_r + a_r$
$11 a_r = 22$
$\Rightarrow a_r = 2 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$

Answer: $2 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ is placed on a rough inclined plane which makes an angle of $37^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. A purely horizontal force $F$ (parallel to the ground) pushes the block towards the incline. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the incline is $0.5$. What is the minimum horizontal force $F$ required to just start moving the block up the incline?
[Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$]
questions.question:
A block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ is placed on a rough inclined plane which makes an angle of $37^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. A purely horizontal force $F$ (parallel to the ground) pushes the block towards the incline. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the incline is $0.5$. What is the minimum horizontal force $F$ required to just start moving the block up the incline?
[Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$]
questions.solution:
Let us resolve the forces parallel and perpendicular to the inclined plane.

The weight $mg$ has a component $mg \sin 37^{\circ}$ down the incline and $mg \cos 37^{\circ}$ perpendicular to the incline (downwards).
The horizontal force $F$ has a component $F \cos 37^{\circ}$ up the incline and $F \sin 37^{\circ}$ perpendicular to the incline (downwards, pressing the block into the surface).

The normal reaction $N$ is:
$N = mg \cos 37^{\circ} + F \sin 37^{\circ}$
$N = (5 \times 10 \times 0.8) + F(0.6) = 40 + 0.6F$

The net driving force pushing the block up the incline is:
$F_{\text{up}} = F \cos 37^{\circ} - mg \sin 37^{\circ}$
$F_{\text{up}} = F(0.8) - (5 \times 10 \times 0.6) = 0.8F - 30$

For the block to just start moving up the incline, this net driving force must overcome the maximum static friction acting down the incline:
$F_{\text{up}} = \mu_s N$
$0.8F - 30 = 0.5(40 + 0.6F)$
$0.8F - 30 = 20 + 0.3F$
$0.8F - 0.3F = 20 + 30$
$0.5F = 50$
$F = 100\text{ N}$

Answer: $100\text{ N}$

questions.q: A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ moving on a horizontal surface with an initial speed of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ enters a rough region at $x = 0$. The retarding force acting on the block in this region is given by $F = -\alpha \sqrt{x}$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant and $x$ is the position in meters. If the block comes to rest exactly at $x = 9\text{ m}$, the value of $\alpha$ (in $\text{N m}^{-1/2}$) is
questions.question: A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ moving on a horizontal surface with an initial speed of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ enters a rough region at $x = 0$. The retarding force acting on the block in this region is given by $F = -\alpha \sqrt{x}$, where $\alpha$ is a positive constant and $x$ is the position in meters. If the block comes to rest exactly at $x = 9\text{ m}$, the value of $\alpha$ (in $\text{N m}^{-1/2}$) is
questions.solution:
According to the work-energy theorem, the net work done on the block equals its change in kinetic energy.

$W = \Delta K$

$W = \int_{0}^{9} F \, dx = \int_{0}^{9} (-\alpha \sqrt{x}) \, dx$

$W = -\alpha \left[ \dfrac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} \right]_{0}^{9} = -\alpha \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right) (9^{3/2} - 0)$

$W = -\alpha \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right) (27) = -18\alpha$

The change in kinetic energy is:

$\Delta K = K_f - K_i = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} m v_0^2$

$\Delta K = -\dfrac{1}{2} (2) (6)^2 = -36\text{ J}$

Equating the work done to the change in kinetic energy:

$-18\alpha = -36 \Rightarrow \alpha = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is suspended in equilibrium by a light string and a light spring attached to a horizontal ceiling. The string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the ceiling, and the spring makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ceiling. If the string is suddenly cut, the magnitude of the initial acceleration of the block immediately after the cut is :
questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is suspended in equilibrium by a light string and a light spring attached to a horizontal ceiling. The string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the ceiling, and the spring makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ceiling. If the string is suddenly cut, the magnitude of the initial acceleration of the block immediately after the cut is :
questions.solution:
Let the tension in the string be $T$ and the spring force be $F_s$.

In the initial equilibrium state, the net force on the block is zero:
$\vec{T} + \vec{F}_s + m\vec{g} = 0$

The string makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal, and the spring makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the horizontal. The angle between the string and the spring is $180^\circ - (30^\circ + 60^\circ) = 90^\circ$.

Resolving forces along the direction of the string, the component of the spring force is zero. The component of gravity along the string is $mg \cos(90^\circ - 30^\circ) = mg \cos(60^\circ)$.

Thus, $T = mg \cos(60^\circ) = \dfrac{mg}{2}$.

When the string is suddenly cut, the tension $T$ becomes zero instantly. However, the spring force $F_s$ does not change instantaneously because the length of the spring has not yet changed.

The new net force on the block is:
$\vec{F}_{net} = \vec{F}_s + m\vec{g}$

From the initial equilibrium condition, we know that $\vec{F}_s + m\vec{g} = -\vec{T}$.

Therefore, the net force immediately after cutting the string is $-\vec{T}$, which has a magnitude of $\dfrac{mg}{2}$.

The initial acceleration of the block is:
$a = \dfrac{F_{net}}{m} = \dfrac{\dfrac{mg}{2}}{m} = \dfrac{g}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{g}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A small block is projected up a rough inclined plane with an initial velocity of $8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. The angle of inclination of the plane is $37^{\circ}$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is $0.25$. The distance travelled by the block along the incline before coming to instantaneous rest is :
[Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$]
questions.question:
A small block is projected up a rough inclined plane with an initial velocity of $8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. The angle of inclination of the plane is $37^{\circ}$ and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is $0.25$. The distance travelled by the block along the incline before coming to instantaneous rest is :
[Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, $\sin 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $\cos 37^{\circ} = \dfrac{4}{5}$]
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the block be $m$.

The forces acting on the block along the incline are the component of gravity downwards and the kinetic friction downwards.
The normal reaction is $N = mg \cos 37^{\circ}$.
The frictional force is $f_k = \mu N = \mu mg \cos 37^{\circ}$.

The net retarding force is $F = mg \sin 37^{\circ} + \mu mg \cos 37^{\circ}$.
The deceleration of the block is:
$a = g \sin 37^{\circ} + \mu g \cos 37^{\circ}$
$a = 10 \times \dfrac{3}{5} + 0.25 \times 10 \times \dfrac{4}{5}$
$a = 6 + 2 = 8 \text{ m s}^{-2}$

Using the third equation of motion, $v^2 = u^2 - 2as$.
Since the block comes to rest, $v = 0$.
$0 = (8)^2 - 2(8)s$
$16s = 64 \Rightarrow s = 4 \text{ m}$.

Answer: $4 \text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block is placed against the inner vertical wall of a hollow cylinder of radius $R$. The cylinder is rotating about its vertical axis. If the coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is $\mu$, what is the minimum angular speed $\omega$ of the cylinder required to prevent the block from sliding down?
questions.question: A small block is placed against the inner vertical wall of a hollow cylinder of radius $R$. The cylinder is rotating about its vertical axis. If the coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is $\mu$, what is the minimum angular speed $\omega$ of the cylinder required to prevent the block from sliding down?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the block be $m$.

The normal force $N$ exerted by the wall of the cylinder provides the necessary centripetal force for the block's circular motion:
$N = m\omega^2 R$

The block is prevented from sliding down by the static friction force $f_s$ acting upwards. For vertical equilibrium, this friction must balance the gravitational force:
$f_s = mg$

The condition for the block not to slide is that the required static friction must not exceed the maximum limiting friction:
$f_s \le \mu N$

Substituting the expressions for $f_s$ and $N$:
$mg \le \mu (m\omega^2 R)$

Cancelling $m$ and rearranging for $\omega^2$:
$\omega^2 \ge \dfrac{g}{\mu R}$

Taking the square root gives the minimum angular speed:
$\omega \ge \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{\mu R}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{\mu R}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A wedge $M$ of mass $35 \mathrm{~kg}$ has a vertical left face and a right face inclined at an angle of $37^\circ$ to the horizontal. A block $m_2$ of mass $5 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed against the vertical left face, and a block $m_1$ of mass $10 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed on the inclined right face. The two blocks are connected by a light, inextensible string that passes over a smooth, light pulley fixed at the top of the wedge. A horizontal force $F$ is applied to the wedge towards the left. All surfaces are frictionless. If block $m_1$ moves down the incline with an acceleration of $2 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$ relative to the wedge, the value of $F$ is
(Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$, $\sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^\circ = \dfrac{4}{5}$)
questions.question:
A wedge $M$ of mass $35 \mathrm{~kg}$ has a vertical left face and a right face inclined at an angle of $37^\circ$ to the horizontal. A block $m_2$ of mass $5 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed against the vertical left face, and a block $m_1$ of mass $10 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed on the inclined right face. The two blocks are connected by a light, inextensible string that passes over a smooth, light pulley fixed at the top of the wedge. A horizontal force $F$ is applied to the wedge towards the left. All surfaces are frictionless. If block $m_1$ moves down the incline with an acceleration of $2 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$ relative to the wedge, the value of $F$ is
(Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$, $\sin 37^\circ = \dfrac{3}{5}$, $\cos 37^\circ = \dfrac{4}{5}$)
questions.solution:
Let $a$ be the acceleration of the wedge to the left.
Since $m_1$ moves down the incline with relative acceleration $a_r = 2 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$, $m_2$ must move up the vertical face with the same relative acceleration $a_r$.

For block $m_2$ in the vertical direction:
$T - m_2 g = m_2 a_r$
$T - 50 = 5(2) \Rightarrow T = 60 \mathrm{~N}$

For block $m_1$ along the incline:
In the frame of the wedge, a pseudo force $m_1 a$ acts on $m_1$ towards the right. Its component down the incline is $m_1 a \cos 37^\circ$.
Equation of motion for $m_1$ down the incline:
$m_1 g \sin 37^\circ + m_1 a \cos 37^\circ - T = m_1 a_r$
$10(10)\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) + 10 a \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right) - 60 = 10(2)$
$60 + 8a - 60 = 20$
$8a = 20 \Rightarrow a = 2.5 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$

Considering the horizontal motion of the entire system:
The absolute horizontal acceleration of $m_1$ (towards the left) is $a - a_r \cos 37^\circ = 2.5 - 2(0.8) = 0.9 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$.
The absolute horizontal acceleration of $M$ and $m_2$ is $a = 2.5 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$ to the left.
Total horizontal force $F = M a + m_2 a + m_1 (a - a_r \cos 37^\circ)$
$F = 35(2.5) + 5(2.5) + 10(0.9)$
$F = 87.5 + 12.5 + 9 = 109 \mathrm{~N}$

Answer: $109 \mathrm{~N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $m$ slides down a rough inclined plane of inclination $\theta$ with a constant downward acceleration $a$. The magnitude of the total contact force exerted by the plane on the block is :
questions.question: A block of mass $m$ slides down a rough inclined plane of inclination $\theta$ with a constant downward acceleration $a$. The magnitude of the total contact force exerted by the plane on the block is :
questions.solution:
Let $N$ be the normal force and $f$ be the frictional force exerted by the incline on the block.

Resolving forces perpendicular to the incline, the block has no acceleration, so:
$N = mg \cos\theta$

Applying Newton's second law along the incline (downwards):
$mg \sin\theta - f = ma \implies f = m(g \sin\theta - a)$

The total contact force is the vector sum of the normal force and the frictional force. Since they are perpendicular, its magnitude is:
$F_{\text{contact}} = \sqrt{N^2 + f^2}$

$F_{\text{contact}} = \sqrt{(mg \cos\theta)^2 + m^2(g \sin\theta - a)^2}$

$F_{\text{contact}} = m\sqrt{g^2 \cos^2\theta + g^2 \sin^2\theta + a^2 - 2ag \sin\theta}$

$F_{\text{contact}} = m\sqrt{g^2 + a^2 - 2ag \sin\theta}$

Answer: $m\sqrt{g^2 + a^2 - 2ag \sin\theta}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $10\text{ kg}$ is being pushed along a rough horizontal surface having a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.2$. The applied force is such that the velocity of the block varies with its position $x$ as $v = 2x$, where $v$ is in $\text{m/s}$ and $x$ is in meters. The magnitude of the applied force when the block is at $x = 3\text{ m}$ is (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$) :
questions.question: A block of mass $10\text{ kg}$ is being pushed along a rough horizontal surface having a coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k = 0.2$. The applied force is such that the velocity of the block varies with its position $x$ as $v = 2x$, where $v$ is in $\text{m/s}$ and $x$ is in meters. The magnitude of the applied force when the block is at $x = 3\text{ m}$ is (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$) :
questions.solution:
The velocity of the block is given by $v = 2x$.

The acceleration $a$ of the block is:
$a = v \dfrac{dv}{dx} = (2x)(2) = 4x$

At $x = 3\text{ m}$, the acceleration is:
$a = 4(3) = 12\text{ m/s}^2$

The net force required to produce this acceleration is:
$F_{\text{net}} = ma = 10 \times 12 = 120\text{ N}$

The kinetic friction acting on the block is:
$f_k = \mu_k mg = 0.2 \times 10 \times 10 = 20\text{ N}$

From Newton's Second Law, the net force is the applied force minus the frictional force:
$F_{\text{net}} = F_{\text{app}} - f_k$

$120 = F_{\text{app}} - 20$

$F_{\text{app}} = 140\text{ N}$

Answer: $140\text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ rests on a rough horizontal surface. A pushing force $F$ is applied to the block, directed downwards at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ below the horizontal. If the coefficient of static friction between the block and the surface is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$, what is the minimum value of $F$ required to just start moving the block?
[Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$]
questions.question:
A block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ rests on a rough horizontal surface. A pushing force $F$ is applied to the block, directed downwards at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ below the horizontal. If the coefficient of static friction between the block and the surface is $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$, what is the minimum value of $F$ required to just start moving the block?
[Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$]
questions.solution:
The applied force $F$ can be resolved into two components: a horizontal component $F \cos 30^{\circ}$ and a vertical component $F \sin 30^{\circ}$ acting downwards.

From the equilibrium of forces in the vertical direction, the normal reaction $N$ is given by:
$N = mg + F \sin 30^{\circ}$
$N = 5 \times 10 + F \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 50 + \dfrac{F}{2}$

For the block to just start moving, the horizontal driving force must equal the maximum static friction:
$F \cos 30^{\circ} = \mu_s N$
$F \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \left(50 + \dfrac{F}{2}\right)$

Multiplying both sides by $2\sqrt{3}$:
$F (\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3}) = 50 + \dfrac{F}{2}$
$3F = 50 + 0.5F$
$2.5F = 50$
$F = \dfrac{50}{2.5} = 20\text{ N}$

Answer: $20\text{ N}$

questions.q: The velocity-time graph of a block projected up a smooth inclined plane is a straight line. The block starts with an initial velocity of $9.8 \text{ m/s}$ at $t=0$ and momentarily comes to rest at $t=2 \text{ s}$. Taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, the angle of inclination of the plane is:
questions.question: The velocity-time graph of a block projected up a smooth inclined plane is a straight line. The block starts with an initial velocity of $9.8 \text{ m/s}$ at $t=0$ and momentarily comes to rest at $t=2 \text{ s}$. Taking $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, the angle of inclination of the plane is:
questions.solution:
From the given velocity-time data, the magnitude of deceleration is:
$a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{9.8 - 0}{2 - 0} = 4.9 \text{ m/s}^2$

For a block moving up a smooth inclined plane of angle $\theta$, the deceleration is provided entirely by the component of gravity along the incline:
$a = g \sin\theta$

Equating the two expressions for deceleration:
$g \sin\theta = 4.9$
$9.8 \sin\theta = 4.9$
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{4.9}{9.8} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Therefore, the angle of inclination is:
$\theta = 30^\circ$

Answer: $30^\circ$

questions.q:
A block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ is placed on a horizontal rough surface and connected to a hanging block of mass $1\text{ kg}$ by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the $4\text{ kg}$ block and the surface varies with the distance $x$ moved by the block as $\mu = \dfrac{x}{8}$. If the system is released from rest at $x = 0$, the maximum speed attained by the blocks is
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question:
A block of mass $4\text{ kg}$ is placed on a horizontal rough surface and connected to a hanging block of mass $1\text{ kg}$ by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the $4\text{ kg}$ block and the surface varies with the distance $x$ moved by the block as $\mu = \dfrac{x}{8}$. If the system is released from rest at $x = 0$, the maximum speed attained by the blocks is
(Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The net driving force on the system is the weight of the hanging block minus the frictional force on the block on the horizontal surface.

$F_{\text{net}} = m_2 g - \mu m_1 g = 1(10) - \left(\dfrac{x}{8}\right)(4)(10) = 10 - 5x$

The acceleration of the system is:

$a = \dfrac{F_{\text{net}}}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{10 - 5x}{4 + 1} = 2 - x$

The speed of the system is maximum when the acceleration becomes zero.

$a = 0 \Rightarrow 2 - x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2\text{ m}$

Using the work-energy theorem for the system from $x = 0$ to $x = 2\text{ m}$:

$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$

$\int_{0}^{2} F_{\text{net}} \, dx = \dfrac{1}{2} (m_1 + m_2) v_{\text{max}}^2 - 0$

$\int_{0}^{2} (10 - 5x) \, dx = \dfrac{1}{2} (5) v_{\text{max}}^2$

$\left[ 10x - \dfrac{5x^2}{2} \right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{5}{2} v_{\text{max}}^2$

$20 - 10 = \dfrac{5}{2} v_{\text{max}}^2$

$10 = \dfrac{5}{2} v_{\text{max}}^2 \Rightarrow v_{\text{max}}^2 = 4 \Rightarrow v_{\text{max}} = 2\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.q: A small block of mass $m$ is attached to one end of a light spring of spring constant $k$ and natural length $L$. The other end of the spring is fixed to a point on a smooth horizontal table. The block is made to rotate in a horizontal circle about the fixed point such that the total length of the spring becomes $nL$ (where $n > 1$). The angular velocity of the block is
questions.question: A small block of mass $m$ is attached to one end of a light spring of spring constant $k$ and natural length $L$. The other end of the spring is fixed to a point on a smooth horizontal table. The block is made to rotate in a horizontal circle about the fixed point such that the total length of the spring becomes $nL$ (where $n > 1$). The angular velocity of the block is
questions.solution:
Let the angular velocity of the block be $\omega$.

The natural length of the spring is $L$ and its stretched length is $nL$.
Elongation in the spring, $x = nL - L = (n-1)L$.

The spring force provides the necessary centripetal force for circular motion.
The radius of the circular path is the total stretched length of the spring, $r = nL$.

Equating the spring force to the centripetal force:
$kx = m\omega^2 r$
$k(n-1)L = m\omega^2(nL)$

Solving for $\omega$:
$\omega^2 = \dfrac{k(n-1)L}{mnL} = \dfrac{k(n-1)}{mn}$
$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k(n-1)}{mn}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{k(n-1)}{mn}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A heavy payload of mass $40\text{ kg}$ is to be lifted vertically from rest using a cable. The cable has a maximum breaking strength of $480\text{ N}$. What is the minimum time required to lift the payload to a height of $9\text{ m}$ without snapping the cable? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question: A heavy payload of mass $40\text{ kg}$ is to be lifted vertically from rest using a cable. The cable has a maximum breaking strength of $480\text{ N}$. What is the minimum time required to lift the payload to a height of $9\text{ m}$ without snapping the cable? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
To find the minimum time, the payload must be lifted with the maximum possible upward acceleration.

Let $a_{\text{max}}$ be the maximum safe upward acceleration. The forces acting on the payload are tension $T$ upwards and weight $mg$ downwards.

Using Newton's second law for upward motion:
$T - mg = ma$

For maximum acceleration, the tension will be at its maximum limit, $T_{\text{max}} = 480\text{ N}$.
$480 - 40(10) = 40 a_{\text{max}}$
$480 - 400 = 40 a_{\text{max}}$
$80 = 40 a_{\text{max}}$
$a_{\text{max}} = 2\text{ m s}^{-2}$

Now, apply the kinematic equation for constant acceleration to find the time taken to cover a height $h = 9\text{ m}$ starting from rest ($u = 0$):
$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$
$9 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(2)t^2$
$9 = t^2$
$t = 3\text{ s}$

The minimum time required is $3\text{ s}$.

Answer: $3\text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is projected upwards along a rough inclined plane of angle $45^{\circ}$. If the retardation of the block is $g$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is
questions.question: A block is projected upwards along a rough inclined plane of angle $45^{\circ}$. If the retardation of the block is $g$, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is
questions.solution:
When the block moves up the incline, both the component of gravity and kinetic friction act downwards along the plane.

The equation of motion is:
$ma = mg \sin 45^{\circ} + \mu_k mg \cos 45^{\circ}$

Given that retardation $a = g$:
$g = g \left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) + \mu_k g \left( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)$

$1 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{\mu_k}{\sqrt{2}}$

$\sqrt{2} = 1 + \mu_k$

$\mu_k = \sqrt{2} - 1$

Answer: $\sqrt{2}-1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small block is pressed against the inner wall of a vertical cylindrical drum of radius $4$ m. The drum is initially rotating at a high speed about its vertical axis but is slowing down with a constant angular deceleration of $6$ rad/s$^2$. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is $0.26$. The block will begin to slip relative to the wall when the angular speed of the drum drops to what value? (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.question: A small block is pressed against the inner wall of a vertical cylindrical drum of radius $4$ m. The drum is initially rotating at a high speed about its vertical axis but is slowing down with a constant angular deceleration of $6$ rad/s$^2$. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the wall is $0.26$. The block will begin to slip relative to the wall when the angular speed of the drum drops to what value? (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
questions.solution:
The normal force $N$ provides the centripetal force for the block:

$N = m \omega^2 R$

Because the drum is decelerating, the block experiences a tangential acceleration $a_t = \alpha R$. Thus, the static friction must provide two perpendicular forces along the surface of the wall:
1. A vertical force to balance gravity: $f_y = mg$
2. A horizontal tangential force to provide the deceleration: $f_t = m a_t = m \alpha R$

The total required static friction $f$ is the vector sum of these two perpendicular components:

$f = \sqrt{f_y^2 + f_t^2} = \sqrt{(mg)^2 + (m \alpha R)^2} = m \sqrt{g^2 + (\alpha R)^2}$

The block begins to slip when this required friction equals the maximum static friction $f_{max} = \mu N$:

$m \sqrt{g^2 + (\alpha R)^2} = \mu (m \omega^2 R)$

Cancelling the mass $m$ and solving for $\omega^2$:

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{\sqrt{g^2 + (\alpha R)^2}}{\mu R}$

First, calculate the tangential acceleration term $\alpha R$:

$\alpha R = 6 \times 4 = 24$ m/s$^2$

Now substitute the values into the equation:

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{\sqrt{10^2 + 24^2}}{0.26 \times 4}$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{\sqrt{100 + 576}}{1.04}$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{\sqrt{676}}{1.04}$

$\omega^2 = \dfrac{26}{1.04}$

$\omega^2 = 25$

$\omega = 5$ rad/s

Answer: $5$ rad/s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block starting from rest slides down a rough inclined plane of angle $30^{\circ}$. The time taken by the block to slide down a certain distance on this rough incline is twice the time it would take to slide down the same distance on a perfectly smooth incline of the same angle. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the rough incline is :
questions.question: A block starting from rest slides down a rough inclined plane of angle $30^{\circ}$. The time taken by the block to slide down a certain distance on this rough incline is twice the time it would take to slide down the same distance on a perfectly smooth incline of the same angle. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the rough incline is :
questions.solution:
Let the distance be $d$. For a block starting from rest, the distance covered is given by $d = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

This implies that the acceleration $a$ is inversely proportional to the square of the time taken, so $\dfrac{a_{\text{smooth}}}{a_{\text{rough}}} = \left(\dfrac{t_{\text{rough}}}{t_{\text{smooth}}}\right)^2$.

Given $t_{\text{rough}} = 2 t_{\text{smooth}}$, we have $a_{\text{smooth}} = 4 a_{\text{rough}}$.

The acceleration on the smooth incline is:
$a_{\text{smooth}} = g \sin 30^{\circ} = \dfrac{g}{2}$

The acceleration on the rough incline is:
$a_{\text{rough}} = g(\sin 30^{\circ} - \mu_k \cos 30^{\circ}) = g\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \mu_k \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

Substituting these into the relation $a_{\text{smooth}} = 4 a_{\text{rough}}$:
$\dfrac{g}{2} = 4g\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \mu_k \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

$\dfrac{1}{2} = 2 - 2\sqrt{3}\mu_k$

$2\sqrt{3}\mu_k = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$\mu_k = \dfrac{3}{4\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An elastic cord has an unstretched length of $30\text{ cm}$. When subjected to a tension $T$, its length becomes $35\text{ cm}$. When the tension is further increased by an amount $\Delta T$, the length of the cord becomes $50\text{ cm}$. If $\Delta T = xT$, the value of $x$ is _____.
questions.question: An elastic cord has an unstretched length of $30\text{ cm}$. When subjected to a tension $T$, its length becomes $35\text{ cm}$. When the tension is further increased by an amount $\Delta T$, the length of the cord becomes $50\text{ cm}$. If $\Delta T = xT$, the value of $x$ is _____.
questions.solution:
Let the force constant of the elastic cord be $k$.

The unstretched length is $L_0 = 30\text{ cm}$.

In the first case, the extension is $x_1 = 35 - 30 = 5\text{ cm}$.
By Hooke's law, $T = k(5)$.

In the second case, the total tension is $T + \Delta T$ and the total extension is $x_2 = 50 - 30 = 20\text{ cm}$.
So, $T + \Delta T = k(20)$.

Dividing the two equations:
$\dfrac{T + \Delta T}{T} = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4$

$1 + \dfrac{\Delta T}{T} = 4$
$\Delta T = 3T$

Comparing with $\Delta T = xT$, we get $x = 3$.

Answer: $3$

questions.q:
A conveyor belt is inclined at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal and moves upwards at a constant speed of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$. A block is gently placed on the belt and slips for some time before catching up to the belt's speed. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the belt is $\sqrt{3}$, the distance travelled by the conveyor belt during the time the block slips on it is:
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.question:
A conveyor belt is inclined at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal and moves upwards at a constant speed of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$. A block is gently placed on the belt and slips for some time before catching up to the belt's speed. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the belt is $\sqrt{3}$, the distance travelled by the conveyor belt during the time the block slips on it is:
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
When the block is gently placed on the moving belt, its initial velocity is zero.

The kinetic friction acts upwards along the incline to accelerate the block, while the component of gravity acts downwards along the incline.

The net acceleration of the block up the incline is given by:
$a = \mu g \cos\theta - g \sin\theta$

Substituting the given values:
$a = \sqrt{3} \times 10 \times \cos 30^{\circ} - 10 \times \sin 30^{\circ}$

$a = 10\sqrt{3} \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - 10 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 15 - 5 = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$

The time taken for the block to reach the belt's speed ($v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$) is:
$t = \dfrac{v}{a} = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6\text{ s}$

The distance travelled by the conveyor belt moving at constant speed during this time is:
$s_{\text{belt}} = v \times t = 6 \times 0.6 = 3.6\text{ m}$.

Answer: $3.6\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A toy water rocket contains $2\text{ kg}$ of water. It ejects all the water at a constant rate over a time interval of $4\text{ s}$, experiencing an average thrust force of $15\text{ N}$. The relative velocity of the ejected water is:
questions.question: A toy water rocket contains $2\text{ kg}$ of water. It ejects all the water at a constant rate over a time interval of $4\text{ s}$, experiencing an average thrust force of $15\text{ N}$. The relative velocity of the ejected water is:
questions.solution:
The thrust force $F$ exerted on the rocket due to the ejection of water is given by:

$F = v_{\text{rel}} \dfrac{\Delta m}{\Delta t}$

where $v_{\text{rel}}$ is the relative velocity of the ejected water, $\Delta m$ is the mass of water ejected, and $\Delta t$ is the time interval.

Given:
$F = 15\text{ N}$
$\Delta m = 2\text{ kg}$
$\Delta t = 4\text{ s}$

Substitute the given values into the formula:

$15 = v_{\text{rel}} \left(\dfrac{2}{4}\right)$

$15 = v_{\text{rel}} \times 0.5$

$v_{\text{rel}} = \dfrac{15}{0.5} = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $10$ kg is pushed from rest on a rough horizontal floor by a constant force of $100$ N acting at an angle of $37^\circ$ downwards from the horizontal. If the block travels a distance of $8$ m in $2$ s, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$, $\sin 37^\circ = 0.6$, $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$):
questions.question: A block of mass $10$ kg is pushed from rest on a rough horizontal floor by a constant force of $100$ N acting at an angle of $37^\circ$ downwards from the horizontal. If the block travels a distance of $8$ m in $2$ s, the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is (Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$, $\sin 37^\circ = 0.6$, $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$):
questions.solution:
From the second equation of motion,

$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$

$\Rightarrow 8 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}a(2)^2$

$\Rightarrow a = 4$ m/s$^2$

Resolving the applied force into horizontal and vertical components:

Horizontal component, $F_x = 100 \cos 37^\circ = 100 \times 0.8 = 80$ N

Vertical component (downwards), $F_y = 100 \sin 37^\circ = 100 \times 0.6 = 60$ N

Applying Newton's second law in the vertical direction to find the normal reaction $N$:

$N = mg + F_y = 10 \times 10 + 60 = 160$ N

Applying Newton's second law in the horizontal direction:

$F_x - \mu_k N = ma$

$\Rightarrow 80 - \mu_k(160) = 10 \times 4$

$\Rightarrow 160\mu_k = 40$

$\Rightarrow \mu_k = 0.25$

Answer: $0.25$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small bob of mass $m$ is suspended from a rigid ceiling by a light spring of natural length $L$ and spring constant $k$. The bob is made to move in a horizontal circle with a constant angular speed $\omega$, acting as a conical pendulum. The cosine of the angle $\theta$ that the spring makes with the vertical is
questions.question: A small bob of mass $m$ is suspended from a rigid ceiling by a light spring of natural length $L$ and spring constant $k$. The bob is made to move in a horizontal circle with a constant angular speed $\omega$, acting as a conical pendulum. The cosine of the angle $\theta$ that the spring makes with the vertical is
questions.solution:
Let the stretched length of the spring during the motion be $L'$.
The radius of the horizontal circular path is $r = L' \sin\theta$.

Let $T$ be the tension in the spring. The horizontal component of tension provides the centripetal force:
$T \sin\theta = m\omega^2 r$
$T \sin\theta = m\omega^2 (L' \sin\theta)$
$T = m\omega^2 L'$

From Hooke's Law, the tension is also given by the elongation of the spring:
$T = k(L' - L)$

Equating the two expressions for tension:
$m\omega^2 L' = k(L' - L)$
$L'(k - m\omega^2) = kL$
$L' = \dfrac{kL}{k - m\omega^2}$

The vertical component of tension balances the weight of the bob:
$T \cos\theta = mg$
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{mg}{T} = \dfrac{mg}{m\omega^2 L'}$

Substituting the expression for $L'$:
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{mg}{m\omega^2 \left( \dfrac{kL}{k - m\omega^2} \right)}$
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{mg(k - m\omega^2)}{k m \omega^2 L}$

Answer: $\dfrac{mg(k - m\omega^2)}{k m \omega^2 L}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block is suspended in equilibrium by two light strings attached to a horizontal ceiling. The first string makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the ceiling. If the tension in the second string is $\sqrt{2}$ times the tension in the first string, the angle made by the second string with the ceiling is :
questions.question: A block is suspended in equilibrium by two light strings attached to a horizontal ceiling. The first string makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the ceiling. If the tension in the second string is $\sqrt{2}$ times the tension in the first string, the angle made by the second string with the ceiling is :
questions.solution:
Let the tension in the first string be $T_1$ and the tension in the second string be $T_2$.

The first string makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the horizontal ceiling, and the second string makes an unknown angle $\theta$ with the ceiling.

For the block to be in horizontal equilibrium, the horizontal components of the tensions in the two strings must be equal and opposite.

$T_1 \cos(45^\circ) = T_2 \cos(\theta)$

It is given that $T_2 = \sqrt{2} T_1$. Substituting this into the equilibrium equation gives:

$T_1 \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = (\sqrt{2} T_1) \cos(\theta)$

Dividing both sides by $T_1$ (since $T_1 \neq 0$):

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} \cos(\theta)$

$\cos(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\theta = 60^\circ$

Answer: $60^\circ$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is attached to one end of a spring of spring constant $200\text{ N m}^{-1}$, while the other end of the spring is fixed to a point on a smooth horizontal table. The block is made to move in a horizontal circle about the fixed point. If the extension in the spring during this motion is one-third of its natural length, the constant angular speed of the block is:
questions.question: A block of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is attached to one end of a spring of spring constant $200\text{ N m}^{-1}$, while the other end of the spring is fixed to a point on a smooth horizontal table. The block is made to move in a horizontal circle about the fixed point. If the extension in the spring during this motion is one-third of its natural length, the constant angular speed of the block is:
questions.solution:
Let the natural length of the spring be $l$. The extension in the spring is given as $x = \dfrac{l}{3}$.

The radius of the circular path is the total length of the stretched spring, $R = l + x = l + \dfrac{l}{3} = \dfrac{4l}{3}$.

The centripetal force required for circular motion is provided by the spring force:
$kx = mR\omega^2$

Substituting the values:
$k\left(\dfrac{l}{3}\right) = m\left(\dfrac{4l}{3}\right)\omega^2$

Cancelling $l/3$ from both sides:
$k = 4m\omega^2$

Given $k = 200\text{ N m}^{-1}$ and $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$:
$200 = 4(0.5)\omega^2$
$200 = 2\omega^2$
$\omega^2 = 100$
$\omega = 10\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Answer: $10\text{ rad s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is moving along a straight line with an initial velocity of $9\text{ m/s}$. It is subjected to a retarding force given by $F = -3\sqrt{v}\text{ N}$, where $v$ is the instantaneous velocity of the block in $\text{m/s}$. The total distance traveled by the block before it comes to a complete stop is:
questions.question: A block of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is moving along a straight line with an initial velocity of $9\text{ m/s}$. It is subjected to a retarding force given by $F = -3\sqrt{v}\text{ N}$, where $v$ is the instantaneous velocity of the block in $\text{m/s}$. The total distance traveled by the block before it comes to a complete stop is:
questions.solution:
From Newton's Second Law, the force on the block is $F = ma$.

Since we need to find the distance, we write the acceleration $a$ as $v \dfrac{dv}{dx}$.
Thus, $m \left(v \dfrac{dv}{dx}\right) = F$

Substituting the given values $m = 2\text{ kg}$ and $F = -3\sqrt{v}$:
$2 v \dfrac{dv}{dx} = -3\sqrt{v}$

Separating the variables:
$2 \sqrt{v} dv = -3 dx$

We integrate both sides. The block's velocity goes from $v_0 = 9\text{ m/s}$ to $v = 0$, and the distance goes from $x = 0$ to $x = x_f$:
$\int_{9}^{0} 2 v^{1/2} dv = \int_{0}^{x_f} -3 dx$

$2 \left[ \dfrac{v^{3/2}}{3/2} \right]_{9}^{0} = -3 [x]_{0}^{x_f}$

$\dfrac{4}{3} \left( 0 - 9^{3/2} \right) = -3 x_f$

Since $9^{3/2} = (3^2)^{3/2} = 27$:
$\dfrac{4}{3} (-27) = -3 x_f$

$-36 = -3 x_f \implies x_f = 12\text{ m}$.

The total distance traveled by the block is $12\text{ m}$.

Answer: $12\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_1 > m_2$) are connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. The system is released from rest. If the heavier mass $m_1$ falls a distance $h$ in time $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{6h}{g}}$, then the ratio of their masses $\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}$ is
questions.question: Two blocks of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_1 > m_2$) are connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. The system is released from rest. If the heavier mass $m_1$ falls a distance $h$ in time $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{6h}{g}}$, then the ratio of their masses $\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}$ is
questions.solution:
From the kinematic equation for uniformly accelerated motion starting from rest:
$h = \dfrac{1}{2} a t^2$

Substitute the given time $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{6h}{g}}$ into the equation:
$h = \dfrac{1}{2} a \left( \dfrac{6h}{g} \right)$

Simplifying this gives:
$h = \dfrac{3ah}{g}$
$a = \dfrac{g}{3}$

For an Atwood machine, the acceleration of the system is given by:
$a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2} g$

Equating the two expressions for acceleration:
$\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2} g = \dfrac{g}{3}$

$\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Cross-multiplying yields:
$3(m_1 - m_2) = m_1 + m_2$
$3m_1 - 3m_2 = m_1 + m_2$
$2m_1 = 4m_2$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A suitcase is gently placed on a horizontal conveyor belt. It leaves a skid mark of length $2.5\text{ m}$ on the belt before it stops slipping and moves along with the belt. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the suitcase and the belt is $0.5$, the speed of the conveyor belt is:
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.question:
A suitcase is gently placed on a horizontal conveyor belt. It leaves a skid mark of length $2.5\text{ m}$ on the belt before it stops slipping and moves along with the belt. If the coefficient of kinetic friction between the suitcase and the belt is $0.5$, the speed of the conveyor belt is:
[Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
The acceleration of the suitcase due to kinetic friction is $a = \mu g = 0.5 \times 10 = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

The length of the skid mark represents the relative distance $s_{\text{rel}}$ slipped by the suitcase on the belt.

The initial relative velocity of the belt with respect to the suitcase is $u_{\text{rel}} = v$ (where $v$ is the speed of the belt).

The final relative velocity when slipping stops is $v_{\text{rel}} = 0$.

Using the kinematic equation for relative motion:
$v_{\text{rel}}^2 = u_{\text{rel}}^2 - 2 a s_{\text{rel}}$

$0 = v^2 - 2(5)(2.5)$

$v^2 = 25 \Rightarrow v = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$

When the same force $F$ is applied to pull the block at the same angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal, the normal reaction becomes $90\text{ N}$. The mass of the block is (Given $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.question: A block is placed on a horizontal surface. When a force $F$ is applied to push the block at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal, the normal reaction from the surface is $150\text{ N}$. When the same force $F$ is applied to pull the block at the same angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal, the normal reaction becomes $90\text{ N}$. The mass of the block is (Given $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
When the block is pushed, the vertical component of the force acts downwards. For vertical equilibrium:
$N_1 = mg + F \sin 30^{\circ} = 150$

When the block is pulled, the vertical component of the force acts upwards. For vertical equilibrium:
$N_2 = mg - F \sin 30^{\circ} = 90$

Adding the two equations, we get:
$N_1 + N_2 = 2mg$
$150 + 90 = 2mg$
$240 = 2m(10)$
$20m = 240 \implies m = 12\text{ kg}$

Answer: $12\text{ kg}$

The turntable, initially at rest, begins to rotate with a constant angular acceleration of $3\text{ rad/s}^2$. If the coefficient of static friction between the coin and the turntable is $0.5$, at what time will the coin just begin to slip? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.question: A small coin is placed at a distance of $1\text{ m}$ from the center of a horizontal turntable. The turntable, initially at rest, begins to rotate with a constant angular acceleration of $3\text{ rad/s}^2$. If the coefficient of static friction between the coin and the turntable is $0.5$, at what time will the coin just begin to slip? (Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.solution:
The coin undergoes non-uniform circular motion, so it experiences both tangential and radial (centripetal) accelerations.

The tangential acceleration $a_t$ is constant:
$a_t = \alpha R = (3)(1) = 3\text{ m/s}^2$

The angular velocity at time $t$ is $\omega = \alpha t = 3t$.
The radial acceleration $a_r$ at time $t$ is:
$a_r = \omega^2 R = (3t)^2(1) = 9t^2\text{ m/s}^2$

The net acceleration of the coin is the vector sum of these two perpendicular components:
$a_{net} = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_r^2} = \sqrt{3^2 + (9t^2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 81t^4}$

The force required to provide this acceleration is $m a_{net}$. This force is provided by static friction. The coin will just begin to slip when this required force equals the maximum limiting static friction:
$m a_{net} = \mu mg$
$a_{net} = \mu g$

Substituting the given values ($\mu = 0.5$, $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
$\sqrt{9 + 81t^4} = 0.5 \times 10 = 5$

Squaring both sides:
$9 + 81t^4 = 25$
$81t^4 = 16$
$t^4 = \dfrac{16}{81}$

Taking the fourth root gives:
$t = \dfrac{2}{3}\text{ s}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ s}$

questions.q: A block of mass $8\text{ kg}$ is placed on a smooth horizontal floor. It is pulled by a uniform heavy rope of mass $4\text{ kg}$ and length $2\text{ m}$ attached to it. A constant horizontal force of $60\text{ N}$ is applied to the free end of the rope. The tension in the rope at a distance of $0.5\text{ m}$ from the block is:
questions.question: A block of mass $8\text{ kg}$ is placed on a smooth horizontal floor. It is pulled by a uniform heavy rope of mass $4\text{ kg}$ and length $2\text{ m}$ attached to it. A constant horizontal force of $60\text{ N}$ is applied to the free end of the rope. The tension in the rope at a distance of $0.5\text{ m}$ from the block is:
questions.solution:
The total mass of the system is the sum of the mass of the block and the mass of the rope.
$M_{\text{total}} = 8\text{ kg} + 4\text{ kg} = 12\text{ kg}$

The common acceleration of the system is:
$a = \dfrac{F}{M_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{60}{12} = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$

We need to find the tension at a point in the rope which is $0.5\text{ m}$ away from the block. The mass of this $0.5\text{ m}$ segment of the rope is:
$m_{\text{segment}} = \left(\dfrac{4\text{ kg}}{2\text{ m}}\right) \times 0.5\text{ m} = 1\text{ kg}$

The total mass being pulled by the tension at this point (the trailing mass) includes the block and the $0.5\text{ m}$ segment of the rope:
$M_{\text{trailing}} = 8\text{ kg} + 1\text{ kg} = 9\text{ kg}$

The tension $T$ at this point provides the acceleration for the trailing mass:
$T = M_{\text{trailing}} \times a = 9 \times 5 = 45\text{ N}$

Answer: $45\text{ N}$
